title: Chemical Changes and Reactions
tagline: How substances change into new substances — combination, decomposition, displacement, double decomposition, and the energy changes that accompany them.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Chemistry syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: A chemical change produces a new substance with new properties; a physical change does not. This chapter classifies the common types of chemical reaction — combination, decomposition, displacement and double decomposition — and examines the evidence that tells you a reaction has happened: gas evolution, colour change, precipitate formation and temperature change. You will also connect reactions to energy changes, learning why combustion and neutralisation release heat while thermal decomposition absorbs it, and practise writing word and chemical equations for each type.

facts.label: Evidence of reaction
facts.value: Gas evolution, colour change, precipitate, temperature change, change in mass

facts.label: Energy terms
facts.value: Exothermic releases heat; endothermic absorbs heat

blocks.text: A physical change alters the form or state of a substance without creating a new substance: ice melts, water evaporates, salt dissolves. The composition of the material stays the same and many physical changes are reversible. A chemical change produces one or more new substances whose composition and properties differ from the reactants: iron rusts, milk sours, magnesium burns. Chemical changes are usually harder to reverse and are accompanied by observable evidence — a gas may bubble off, a solid precipitate may form, a colour may change, or the temperature may rise or fall.

items.meaning: A change that produces new substance(s) with new chemical properties, such as burning magnesium to give magnesium oxide.
The process in which reactants are converted into products; the reactants are the starting substances and the products the substances formed.
A change that releases heat to the surroundings, causing the temperature of the surroundings to rise.
A change that absorbs heat from the surroundings, causing the temperature to fall.

items: Signs a chemical change has occurred: gas bubbles in a liquid without boiling, a precipitate forming, an unmistakable colour change, light or flame, or a temperature change with no obvious cause.
Burning a candle shows both changes at once: melting wax is physical, wax vapour burning is chemical.
Dissolving sugar is physical — the sugar can be recovered by evaporation and no new substance forms.
Rusting of iron is chemical — hydrated iron(III) oxide forms and cannot be simply separated back into iron and oxygen.

items.text: Heating blue copper(II) carbonate gives black copper(II) oxide and carbon dioxide gas.
items.note: Colour change plus gas evolution — two independent signs of a chemical change.

items.text: Adding dilute acid to a carbonate fizzes: the gas is carbon dioxide.
items.note: Effervescence without heating indicates a reaction producing a gas.

learn.title: Combination, decomposition, displacement and double decomposition

blocks.text: In a combination (synthesis) reaction two or more substances join to form a single product: A + B -> AB. Burning magnesium, calcium oxide with water, and sulphur dioxide with water are typical examples. In a decomposition reaction a single compound breaks down, usually with heat, light or electricity: AB -> A + B. Thermal decomposition of limestone, electrolysis of water and the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide are standard cases. In a displacement reaction a more reactive element pushes a less reactive one out of a compound: A + BC -> AC + B — iron displacing copper from copper sulphate is the classic laboratory example. In a double decomposition (double displacement) two compounds exchange partners, and if a precipitate, gas or weak electrolyte forms, the reaction proceeds: AB + CD -> AD + CB.

items: Combination is usually exothermic: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO releases light and heat.
Decomposition is endothermic because bonds must be broken: CaCO3 ->(heat) CaO + CO2.
Displacement depends on the reactivity series: a metal higher in the series displaces a lower one from its salt solution.
Double decomposition in the lab usually shows as a precipitate: silver nitrate plus sodium chloride gives white silver chloride.
Displacement and double decomposition both involve two compounds reacting; check whether elements swap or partners swap.

items.text: Combination: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO, and CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2.
items.note: Two reactants, one product — the defining feature of combination.
One reactant, two or more products; energy input is almost always required.
Iron is more reactive than copper, so it takes the sulphate partner; the blue colour fades as copper deposits.

items.text: Double decomposition: AgNO3 + NaCl -> AgCl (downward arrow) + NaNO3.
items.note: Silver chloride is the white precipitate that drives the reaction; no element is displaced — the partners exchange.

items.meaning: Two or more reactants combine to form a single product: A + B -> AB.
One compound breaks down into simpler substances, usually requiring heat, light or electricity.
A more reactive element replaces a less reactive element in a compound.
Two compounds exchange partners, often producing a precipitate, gas or water.
An insoluble solid that forms when two solutions are mixed, showing that a reaction has occurred.

blocks.text: Every chemical reaction involves an energy change. In an exothermic reaction the products hold less energy than the reactants, and the difference is released — usually as heat — so the surroundings warm up. Combustion, respiration and neutralisation are exothermic. In an endothermic reaction the products hold more energy than the reactants, so heat is absorbed and the surroundings cool. Thermal decomposition, photosynthesis and the dissolving of ammonium nitrate in water are endothermic. Energy must be supplied to break bonds in the reactants and is released when bonds form in the products; a reaction is exothermic when the energy released in bond formation exceeds the energy absorbed in bond breaking.

items.text: Burning natural gas: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O releases heat used for cooking.
items.note: Combustion is always exothermic because oxygen is combining with the fuel.

items.text: Thermal decomposition: CaCO3 ->(heat) CaO + CO2 requires continuous heating.
items.note: The reaction stops when the heat source is removed — a quick way to identify an endothermic change.

items: Exothermic: combustion, respiration, neutralisation, most combination reactions.
Endothermic: thermal decomposition, electrolysis, photosynthesis, dissolving ammonium nitrate.
In a reversible reaction, the forward and backward reactions can both occur; conditions such as temperature decide which predominates.
Energy profile wording: exothermic reactions have products lower in energy than reactants; endothermic reactions have products higher.

blocks.text: A complete description of a reaction includes the word equation, the balanced chemical equation with state symbols, and the observation you would record. The state symbols matter: (s) for solids, (l) for liquids, (g) for gases and (aq) for aqueous solutions. When a precipitate forms, a downward arrow after the formula marks it as insoluble. When a gas forms, naming the observation — effervescence, or a specific test such as lime water turning milky — is part of the answer, not an extra detail.

items.text: Copper sulphate solution plus sodium hydroxide: CuSO4(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) -> Cu(OH)2(s) + Na2SO4(aq).
items.note: Observation: pale blue gelatinous precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide — a double decomposition reaction.

items.text: Zinc plus dilute hydrochloric acid: Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> ZnCl2(aq) + H2(g).
items.note: Observation: brisk effervescence; the gas pops with a lighted splint, identifying hydrogen.

items.text: Ammonia plus hydrogen chloride: NH3(g) + HCl(g) -> NH4Cl(s).
items.note: Observation: dense white fumes of ammonium chloride — a combination reaction at room temperature.

items: Always give the observation requested: colour of precipitate, direction of gas test result, or temperature change.
A downward arrow marks an insoluble product in a precipitation reaction.
Include state symbols in equations when the question asks for a complete equation.
Word equation first, then correct formulae, then balancing — in that order.

figures.caption: Figure: Classifying a reaction in four questions
figures.description: Start with the number of reactants and products: two or more into one is combination; one into several is decomposition; an element plus a compound with a new element as product is displacement; two compounds swapping partners with a precipitate is double decomposition.

keyPoints: A chemical change produces new substance(s); a physical change does not.
Evidence of reaction: gas, precipitate, colour change, temperature change, light.
Combination: A + B -> AB, generally exothermic.
Decomposition: AB -> A + B, requires heat, light or electricity.
Displacement: a more reactive element replaces a less reactive one in a compound.
Double decomposition: two compounds exchange partners, usually forming a precipitate.
Exothermic reactions release heat; endothermic reactions absorb heat.
State symbols are (s), (l), (g) and (aq); a downward arrow marks a precipitate.
Observations such as 'brisk effervescence' or 'pale blue precipitate' earn marks in their own right.
examFocus: Type-classification questions need the reasoning as well as the label: state which feature (one product, precipitate, element swap) proves the type.
Energy questions expect both the term (exothermic/endothermic) and the reason in terms of heat released or absorbed.
Equation questions reward state symbols and the precipitate arrow — include them whenever a full equation is asked for.
Observation questions are precise: 'colour changes' is too vague; write 'blue solution fades and a red-brown solid deposits'.

vocabulary.meaning: A starting substance that takes part in a chemical reaction.
A substance produced by a chemical reaction.
Insoluble solid formed when two solutions react.
Breakdown of one compound into simpler substances.

questions.prompt: Which change is a chemical change?
questions.explanation: Rusting produces hydrated iron(III) oxide, a new substance with new properties; the other options only change state or dispersion.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing dissolving, which feels dramatic but produces no new substance.

questions.prompt: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO is an example of which type of reaction?
questions.explanation: Two substances combine to form a single product, which is the defining feature of a combination (synthesis) reaction.
questions.commonMistake: Calling it a displacement reaction because magnesium 'replaces' something; there is only one product, so no displacement occurred.

questions.prompt: In the reaction Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu, which substance has been displaced?
questions.explanation: Iron, being more reactive than copper, takes the place of copper in the sulphate, so copper is displaced and deposits as a red-brown solid.
questions.commonMistake: Saying iron is displaced — iron enters the compound; the element that leaves the compound is the one displaced.

questions.prompt: Which observation would NOT be evidence of a chemical reaction?
options: A colourless gas evolving at room temperature
A white precipitate forming on mixing two solutions
Temperature rising with no heat source applied
A crystal changing size when the solvent evaporates
questions.answer: A crystal changing size when the solvent evaporates
questions.explanation: Recovering a solid by evaporation is a physical change — the same substance is left behind. The other three observations indicate new substances or energy change.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming any visible change is chemical; state changes such as evaporation are physical.

questions.prompt: A reaction that absorbs heat from the surroundings is called:
questions.explanation: Endothermic reactions take in heat, so the surroundings cool; combustion and neutralisation are exothermic.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing the prefixes: 'endo-' means inwards, 'exo-' means outwards.

options: Neutralisation of an acid with an alkali
questions.explanation: Decomposition requires continuous heat input to break bonds, so it absorbs energy; the other three release heat.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming heating something makes it exothermic — the heat supplied is absorbed by the reaction, not released by it.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: AgNO3 + NaCl -> AgCl + NaNO3 is an example of a ________ reaction, and AgCl appears as a ________.
questions.explanation: The two compounds exchange partners and silver chloride is insoluble, so a white precipitate marks the reaction.
questions.commonMistake: Calling it a displacement reaction; no free element is produced, so no element was displaced.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a decomposition reaction requires energy input in the form of ________, ________ or ________ (any three forms).
questions.explanation: Compounds break down only when given energy: limestone needs heat, silver chloride decomposes in light, and water decomposes by electrolysis.
questions.commonMistake: Listing only heat and forgetting that electrolysis (electrical energy) and photographic decomposition (light) are also standard cases.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a physical change and a chemical change with one example of each.
questions.answer: A physical change alters form or state without producing a new substance and is usually reversible — for example, ice melting into water. A chemical change produces a new substance with new properties — for example, iron rusting to form hydrated iron(III) oxide, which cannot be simply reverted.
questions.explanation: The test is whether the composition of the material changes; composition changing means chemical, unchanged means physical.
questions.commonMistake: Describing only what is observed (colour, shape) instead of referring to the composition of the substance.

questions.prompt: Classify each reaction and write a word equation for each: (a) calcium oxide + water (b) zinc + copper sulphate solution (c) silver nitrate solution + sodium chloride solution.
questions.answer: (a) Combination: calcium oxide + water -> calcium hydroxide. (b) Displacement: zinc + copper sulphate -> zinc sulphate + copper. (c) Double decomposition: silver nitrate + sodium chloride -> silver chloride (precipitate) + sodium nitrate.
questions.explanation: In (a) two substances form one product; in (b) an element replaces another in a compound; in (c) two compounds exchange partners with a precipitate forming.
questions.commonMistake: Giving only the reaction type when the question also asks for word equations — both parts must be answered.

questions.prompt: State the main differences between exothermic and endothermic reactions, giving one example of each and one practical observation of each.
questions.answer: Exothermic reactions release heat to the surroundings — the container feels warm; example: neutralisation of an acid by an alkali. Endothermic reactions absorb heat — the container feels cold; example: dissolving ammonium nitrate in water or thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate.
questions.explanation: The direction of heat flow defines the category; the observation of temperature change is how it is detected experimentally.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting the observation; questions typically ask for a difference, an example and an observation for full marks.

questions.prompt: Write the balanced equation for the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate. State the type of reaction, the energy change involved, and two ways the product can be identified.
questions.answer: CaCO3(s) ->(heat) CaO(s) + CO2(g). The reaction is a decomposition (one reactant forming two products) and it is endothermic because heating is required continuously. The solid product, calcium oxide (quicklime), is a white solid that reacts vigorously with water to give an alkaline calcium hydroxide solution; the gas product is carbon dioxide, which turns lime water milky.
questions.explanation: One compound breaking into two identifies decomposition; continuous heating identifies the endothermic energy change; the products are then identified by their characteristic reactions rather than by appearance alone.
questions.commonMistake: Calling it combination because the reverse reaction (CaO + CO2 -> CaCO3) is a combination — the direction written in the equation decides the type.

questions.prompt: A student mixes iron filings with copper sulphate solution and leaves the tube undisturbed. Describe the observations, identify the type of reaction, and explain why this reaction occurs but the reverse does not.
questions.answer: Observations: the blue colour of the copper sulphate solution gradually fades, a red-brown deposit of copper forms on the iron filings, and the solution becomes pale green due to iron(II) sulphate. The reaction is a displacement reaction: Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu. It occurs because iron is more reactive than copper and therefore displaces copper from its salt; the reverse does not occur because copper cannot displace iron from iron sulphate — copper is lower in the reactivity series.
questions.explanation: Every displacement reaction is explained by the reactivity series: the more reactive metal displaces the less reactive one, and the direction cannot be reversed without supplying external energy.
questions.commonMistake: Giving observations without linking them to the substances (blue fading = loss of Cu2+ ions; green tint = formation of Fe2+ ions).

questions.prompt: Why is burning a candle said to involve both a physical and a chemical change?
questions.answer: The wax first melts — a physical change, because it is still the same substance and can resolidify. The melted wax then vaporises, also physical. The wax vapour burns with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water — a chemical change, because new substances form and the process cannot be reversed simply by cooling.
questions.explanation: A single event can contain both change types; the correct analysis separates what happens to the wax itself (state changes) from what happens when it reacts with oxygen (combustion).
questions.commonMistake: Claiming melting is chemical because the candle 'disappears' — mass is conserved; the wax is converted to gas, not destroyed.
